title: Pewaukee is the new sub-breakeven store: True ROAS 0.90 (from 1.25, -0.35) on $595 spend — order revenue fell 48% while spend fell only 28%
detail: Pewaukee produced $534 of tracked online-order revenue (19.2 orders) on $595 spend, the only meaningful True-ROAS decline in the account this period. Real revenue fell $1,027 -> $534 (-48%) while its budget came down just $823 -> $595 (-28%), so the ratio broke below 1.0. It is the 4th-largest spender, so this is real money: roughly $60 of spend beyond tracked order value. Blended ROAS is flat (3.73 vs 3.77) and hides it completely — this is exactly the pattern where a per-store True-ROAS read catches something the blended number never shows. Action: trim Pewaukee ~$150-200/period (raise target ROAS or lower the budget cap) and check the Pewaukee online-ordering funnel for a menu/hours/store-page issue; recheck next week before cutting further. Standing caveat: in-store visits driven by these local ads are not captured here, so 0.90 is the measurable floor, not the full return.

title: Spend still concentrated on the two weakest big stores: Brookfield ($731, TrueROAS 1.21) + Milwaukee ($727, 1.05) take 27% of budget while Middleton (1.89) sits at $462 and State Street (1.47) at $298
detail: The spend ranking remains inverted against measurable order value. Milwaukee has now been flagged three-plus periods running: at $727 it is the #2 spender and returned $764 of tracked orders — a True ROAS of 1.05, the weakest of any store above $400 and drifting down (1.11 prior). Brookfield at $731 returns 1.21. Meanwhile Middleton generated $874 of order revenue on just $462 (1.89, best in the account and up from 1.30), and State Street returned 1.47 (up from 0.94) on only $298. Moving ~$250-300/period out of Milwaukee and Brookfield into Middleton and State Street would buy more tracked order revenue at identical total spend. Action: raise Middleton and State Street budget caps first (they have proven headroom), then trim Milwaukee. If Milwaukee's dine-in volume is the reason to keep funding it, confirm with Toast same-store sales rather than leaving the decision on the online number alone.

title: Account True ROAS recovered to 1.42 (from 1.24) — last week's suspected tracking break did not materialize; close that item
detail: Spend was cut 26% ($7,386 -> $5,455) while tracked online-order revenue fell only 15% ($9,147 -> $7,749), lifting account True ROAS to 1.42, the strongest of the last three periods. The two stores flagged last week as possible GA4 tag failures both rebounded on the newer window: Brookfield 0.67 -> 1.21 and Hilldale 1.15 -> 1.68, and 8 of 11 funded stores improved their True ROAS. That pattern is consistent with GA4 conversion lag and demand normalization, not a broken purchase tag, so the Brookfield/Hilldale tag spot-check can be dropped to a low-priority sanity check. One open question worth confirming: the 26% account-wide spend reduction was broad-based across every store (impressions -30%) and larger than the Top Locations pause alone explains — verify it was an intentional budget decision rather than a budget-pacing or billing side effect.

title: Meta spend jumped 65% to $1,091 (+$431) and is now 17% of all paid spend with zero purchase tracking
detail: Meta rose from its usual ~$660-700/period to $1,091, driven almost entirely by 'brookfield sales 0726' scaling from $19 to $336, plus two new small campus campaigns (UIUC $22, UW $14). Efficiency as traffic actually improved — 3,588 landing-page views at $0.30/LPV vs $0.35 — so the media is buying cheaper clicks. The problem is measurement: all seven campaigns are traffic-objective with no purchase event, so $1,091/period, now one dollar in six of total paid spend, cannot be evaluated on True ROAS the way every Google campaign can. This is the account's largest measurement blind spot and it grew again this period. Action: install the Meta Pixel purchase event on the Toast order-confirmation page so Meta can be judged on the same basis as Google, and confirm the Brookfield scale-up to $336 is intentional. Also still outstanding: migrate off the legacy personal-named ad account (act_35967094).

title: Champaign nearly doubled True ROAS to 0.94 (from 0.47) on a 27% smaller budget — the trim worked, hold it here rather than cutting further
detail: Last period's recommendation was to halve Champaign or verify its ordering funnel. Spend came down $412 -> $299 (-27%) and tracked order revenue went the other way, $193 -> $281 (+46%, 11.6 orders), taking True ROAS from a worst-in-account 0.47 to 0.94 — essentially breakeven on measurable orders and no longer an outlier. The funnel evidently works; the store was simply overfunded relative to its online demand. Action: hold Champaign at roughly the current $300/period and do not cut further this cycle. If it clears 1.0 next period, it is a normal store. Note the new Meta 'UIUC Campus 0826' campaign ($22) also targets this market — keep the two reads separate when judging Champaign's trend.

title: Meta's 'Catering Traffic 0326 video' costs $0.48/LPV — 60% above the $0.30 account average — at $223 spend
detail: Among the seven Meta campaigns, cost per landing-page view clusters tightly between $0.24 and $0.29 (Rewards $0.26, Brookfield $0.28, Branding $0.29, Falafel $0.29, UW $0.24, UIUC $0.27). Catering Traffic sits alone at $0.48 — $223 spend for 468 LPVs — and its click-to-LPV drop-off is the steepest in the set (867 clicks, 605 link clicks, 468 LPVs). It also carried a similar premium last period ($0.60/LPV), so this is a persistent creative/audience efficiency gap, not a one-week blip. Catering is a legitimately different objective from retail traffic, so the higher cost may be acceptable if it drives catering inquiries — but nothing in the account measures that. Action: either refresh the catering creative/audience, or define a catering-inquiry conversion event so the $223 can be judged on something other than LPV cost. Low priority given the dollar size relative to Google's $5,455.
